stem: How is the perplexity of a causal language model on a text defined?

options.text: The share of tokens the model predicts exactly right
options.why: That is next-token accuracy. Perplexity uses the probability given to the true token, not whether it was the top guess.

options.text: The exponential of the average negative log-likelihood per token
options.why: Correct. PPL = exp(mean of -log p(token | previous tokens)), which is exp of the cross-entropy.

options.text: The number of distinct tokens in the vocabulary divided by the sequence length
options.why: Vocabulary size is fixed by the tokenizer and says nothing about how well a model predicts a text.

options.text: The average cosine similarity between the output and a reference answer
options.why: That describes an embedding-similarity metric, not a likelihood-based one.

explanation: Perplexity is the exponentiated average negative log-likelihood of the tokens, equivalently exp(cross-entropy). Lower is better: a perplexity of k means the model is, on average, as unsure as if it picked uniformly among k tokens. It is defined for causal models and is not well defined for masked models like BERT.

stem: If model A has lower perplexity than model B on general web text, model A is guaranteed to be the more helpful chat assistant.

options.text: True
options.why: This is wrong: perplexity measures how well a model predicts text, not whether its answers are helpful, correct or safe.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct. Perplexity rewards predicting the corpus well. Helpfulness depends on instruction following, correctness and style, which need task-level evaluation.

explanation: Perplexity is a useful training and language-modelling signal, but it does not measure helpfulness, factual accuracy or instruction following. Evaluate assistants on the tasks users care about.

stem: What does the HumanEval benchmark measure for code generation?

options.text: How closely generated code matches a reference solution, word for word
options.why: Match-based metrics were rejected by its authors because many different programs are correct.

options.text: How fast the generated code runs on a standard machine
options.why: Runtime is not scored; a sample counts only as correct or incorrect.

options.text: Whether generated functions pass hand-written unit tests
options.why: Correct. It scores functional correctness on 164 hand-written problems with unit tests.

options.text: Whether a model can fix real issues across whole GitHub repositories
options.why: That describes SWE-bench, which uses real repositories and issues, not standalone functions.

explanation: HumanEval has 164 hand-written Python problems, each with a signature, docstring and unit tests (7.7 tests on average). A sample is correct if it passes the tests, and results are reported as pass@k. Its authors found BLEU a poor proxy for functional correctness.

stem: What is benchmark contamination?

options.text: Test questions, or close variants, appearing in a model's training data, which inflates its score
options.why: Correct. The model may recall answers rather than solve the problems.

options.text: Running a benchmark on hardware that has other jobs on it at the same time
options.why: Shared hardware affects speed, not whether scores reflect real ability.

options.text: Using a benchmark that has spelling mistakes in a few of its questions
options.why: Label noise is a quality issue, but it is not what contamination means.

options.text: Mixing questions from several benchmarks into one combined score for reporting
options.why: Aggregating benchmarks can hide detail, but it is not contamination.

explanation: Contamination happens when evaluation data leaks into pretraining or fine-tuning data. Scores then measure memorisation as well as skill. A common symptom is a much higher score on the public test than on a freshly written test of the same style and difficulty.

stem: In LLM-as-a-judge pairwise evaluation, what is **position bias**?

options.text: The judge prefers answers from models that are higher on public leaderboards
options.why: That would be a reputation effect; in a blind comparison the judge does not see model names.

options.text: Favouring an answer because of its slot, often the first
options.why: Correct. Swapping the order can flip the verdict even though the answers are identical.

options.text: The judge gives lower scores to answers that use bullet points
options.why: Format preferences exist, but position bias is specifically about order.

options.text: The judge cannot score answers longer than its context window
options.why: That is a capacity limit, not a bias about order.

explanation: The MT-Bench study documented position bias (favouring a slot, often the first), verbosity bias (favouring longer answers) and self-enhancement bias (favouring its own model's answers). For position bias, the standard fix is to judge both orders and treat inconsistent verdicts as a tie.

stem: What is the difference between offline and online evaluation of an LLM feature?

options.text: Offline runs on a laptop, online runs in the cloud
options.why: The terms are about data and users, not where the code runs.

options.text: Offline uses a fixed dataset; online measures live users
options.why: Correct. Offline is repeatable and cheap; online shows real impact.

options.text: Offline relies only on human raters, while online relies only on automated metrics computed by the serving stack
options.why: Both can use humans or automated metrics; the difference is fixed data versus live traffic.

options.text: Offline is for small models and online is reserved for large frontier models
options.why: Any model can be evaluated both ways.

explanation: Offline evaluation scores a model on a fixed, versioned dataset before release, so changes can be compared quickly and repeatably. Online evaluation (A/B tests, canaries, user feedback, task completion) shows real impact but is slower and noisier. Mature teams use both: offline to gate, online to confirm.

stem: In LLM evaluation, what is a **golden set**?

options.text: The highest-scoring answers your model produced last month, saved as the targets for future versions
options.why: Using your own best outputs as the target would freeze in past mistakes.

options.text: A public leaderboard of the best models
options.why: A leaderboard ranks models; a golden set is your own labelled test data.

options.text: A curated, versioned set of test inputs with expected results
options.why: Correct. It is the stable yardstick for regression testing.

options.text: A list of prompts that are banned from the product
options.why: That is a blocklist, not an evaluation set.

explanation: A golden set is a carefully reviewed collection of representative and tricky inputs with reference answers or rubrics. It is versioned and run on every prompt or model change so regressions are caught before users see them. Keep part of it hidden from prompt tuning so it stays an honest test.

stem: Match each automatic text metric with what it is based on.

options.text: BLEU
options.why: Clipped n-gram precision with a brevity penalty.

options.text: ROUGE-L
options.why: Longest common subsequence between output and reference.

options.text: BERTScore
options.why: Similarity of contextual token embeddings.

options.text: Exact match
options.why: Whether the normalised answer string equals a reference.

prompts.text: Counts how many of the output's n-grams (up to 4-grams by default) appear in a reference, and penalises outputs that are too short
Finds the longest in-order, not necessarily contiguous, word sequence shared with the reference
Matches each token to its most similar token in the other text using contextual embeddings
Scores 1 only when the answer, after lowercasing and removing punctuation and articles, equals a reference

explanation: BLEU is precision-oriented: clipped n-gram precision, geometric mean up to 4-grams, times a brevity penalty. ROUGE is recall-oriented; ROUGE-L uses the longest common subsequence. BERTScore greedily matches tokens by cosine similarity of contextual embeddings, so it can credit paraphrases. Exact match (as in SQuAD) compares normalised strings.

stem: A model's average cross-entropy loss on a held-out text is 2.0 nats per token. What is its perplexity? Round to two decimal places.
explanation: Perplexity = exp(average negative log-likelihood) = e^2.0, about 7.39. If the loss were in bits (log base 2), you would use 2^loss instead. Always check the log base before converting.

stem: Two teams compare perplexity on the same test text. Model A uses a 32k-token vocabulary and model B a 128k-token vocabulary. Why can't the raw per-token perplexities be compared directly?

options.text: Perplexity is only defined for vocabularies smaller than 50k
options.why: There is no such limit; perplexity is defined for any vocabulary size.

options.text: Per-token averages depend on how each tokenizer splits the text
options.why: Correct. Normalise per character or per byte (bits per byte) to compare across tokenizers.

options.text: Larger vocabularies push perplexity towards exactly 1, because each token then carries almost all of the information
options.why: Nothing forces perplexity to 1; it reflects prediction quality and token granularity.

options.text: Perplexity must be computed with a masked language model to be comparable
options.why: The reverse: perplexity is not well defined for masked models.

explanation: Perplexity averages over tokens, and the tokenizer decides what a token is. A model whose tokens are longer predicts fewer, harder units, so its per-token perplexity is not on the same scale. Compare using the same tokenizer, or normalise per character or byte.

stem: Your LLM judge compares two answers and prefers whichever is shown first about 70% of the time. What is the standard mitigation?

options.text: Judge both orders; call a tie if the verdicts disagree
options.why: Correct. This cancels the order effect and exposes judgments that depended only on position.

options.text: Always put your own model's answer second to be fair
options.why: A fixed order keeps the bias; it just moves which side benefits.

options.text: Ask the judge to write a longer, step-by-step explanation of both answers before it decides
options.why: Explanations can help a little, but they do not remove order effects on their own.

options.text: Raise the judge's temperature so verdicts vary more
options.why: Random noise does not remove a systematic preference; it only adds variance.

explanation: MT-Bench's authors swapped answer positions and counted a win only if the judge preferred the same answer in both orders; otherwise it was a tie. Randomising order across the dataset also balances the bias, and few-shot judge prompts improved consistency at extra cost.

stem: Match each benchmark with what it mainly tests.

options.text: MMLU
options.why: Multiple-choice knowledge across 57 subjects.

options.text: GSM8K
options.why: Grade-school maths word problems.

options.text: SWE-bench
options.why: Resolving real GitHub issues in Python repositories.

options.text: MT-Bench
options.why: Multi-turn open-ended questions graded by an LLM judge.

prompts.text: Four-option questions spanning subjects from elementary maths to law
About 8.5K multi-step arithmetic word problems with numeric answers
Producing a patch that makes failing repository tests pass without breaking others
80 multi-turn prompts in categories such as writing, reasoning and coding

explanation: MMLU checks breadth of knowledge with four-option questions across 57 subjects. GSM8K has about 8.5K grade-school maths word problems. SWE-bench has 2,294 tasks from 12 Python repositories, scored by running tests that must go from failing to passing. MT-Bench has 80 multi-turn questions in 8 categories, graded by a strong LLM judge.

stem: A QA model predicts "The Eiffel Tower, in Paris." and the reference answer is "Eiffel Tower". Using SQuAD-style scoring (lowercase, strip punctuation and the articles a/an/the, then compare tokens), what are exact match and token F1?

options.text: Exact match 1, F1 1.0
options.why: After normalisation the prediction is "eiffel tower in paris", which is not equal to "eiffel tower".

options.text: Exact match 0, F1 0.67
options.why: Correct. Precision is 2/4 and recall 2/2, so F1 = 2 x 0.5 x 1 / 1.5, about 0.67.

options.text: Exact match 0, F1 0.5
options.why: 0.5 is the precision only; F1 is the harmonic mean of precision (0.5) and recall (1.0).

options.text: Exact match 0, F1 0, as articles are kept
options.why: Two tokens overlap, so F1 cannot be zero.

explanation: SQuAD normalisation lowercases, removes punctuation and articles, and collapses spaces. Exact match needs identical normalised strings, so extra words score 0. Token F1 gives partial credit: overlap 2, precision 2/4, recall 2/2, F1 = 0.67. With several references, take the maximum over them.

stem: Which two pairings of task and evaluation metric are sound? (Choose two.)

options.text: Classifying support tickets into five fixed labels: exact-match accuracy on a labelled set
options.why: Fixed labels have one correct answer, so exact match (with per-class breakdowns) fits.

options.text: Generating Python functions: pass@k against unit tests
options.why: Unit tests check functional correctness, which is what matters for code.

options.text: Checking factual accuracy of chatbot answers: BLEU against one reference answer
options.why: BLEU measures n-gram overlap; a correct answer worded differently scores low and a wrong answer with shared words scores high.

options.text: Judging summary quality: the model's perplexity on its own summary
options.why: Low perplexity on its own output means the text is predictable to the model, not that the summary is faithful or useful.

options.text: Checking that generated code is correct: ROUGE against a reference solution
options.why: Many correct programs look different from the reference; overlap does not test behaviour.

explanation: Pick metrics that check what success means for the task: exact match or accuracy for closed labels, execution-based pass@k for code, and rubric-based or faithfulness grading for open-ended text. Overlap and likelihood metrics are weak proxies for correctness in open-ended generation.

stem: How does Chatbot Arena produce its model rankings?

options.text: Experts grade each model's answers on a fixed list of 1,000 questions
options.why: The prompts come from users, not a fixed expert-written list.

options.text: Each model's rating is a weighted average of its MMLU, GSM8K and HumanEval accuracy, updated every month
options.why: Arena rankings come from human votes, not static benchmark scores.

options.text: A model judge rates every answer from 1 to 10
options.why: That describes single-answer grading as in MT-Bench, not the Arena.

options.text: Users vote between two anonymous models' answers to their own prompt, and the votes are fitted with a Bradley-Terry model
options.why: Correct. Identities are revealed only after the vote, and Bradley-Terry coefficients turn pairwise wins into ratings.

explanation: Chatbot Arena crowdsources pairwise comparisons: a user chats with two anonymous models and votes for the better answer. Earlier versions reported online Elo; the paper switched to Bradley-Terry coefficients for better statistical estimation, with confidence intervals. It reflects broad user preference, which may differ from your product's needs.

stem: BERTScore can give credit to a paraphrase that BLEU scores poorly, because it matches tokens by the similarity of their contextual embeddings rather than by exact n-grams.

options.text: True
options.why: Correct. BERTScore greedily pairs each token with its most similar token in the other text, so synonyms and rewordings can still score well.

options.text: False
options.why: This is wrong: unlike BLEU's exact n-gram matching, BERTScore compares embeddings, so different words with similar meaning can match.

explanation: BERTScore computes token-level cosine similarities between contextual embeddings, greedily matches tokens, and reports precision, recall and F1 (optionally idf-weighted and rescaled). It handles paraphrase better than BLEU or ROUGE, but it still needs a reference and is not a factuality check.

stem: You want to track the quality of a single production prompt week by week, with no second system to compare against. Which judging setup fits?

options.text: Pairwise comparison against a random older answer each week
options.why: Comparing against a changing baseline makes week-to-week numbers hard to interpret.

options.text: Pointwise grading against a fixed rubric and a frozen judge
options.why: Correct. Absolute scores against a stable rubric give a trend you can compare over time.

options.text: Pairwise comparison against the same answer, to check consistency
options.why: Comparing an answer with itself gives no quality signal.

options.text: Ranking all answers of the week from best to worst and reporting the median rank as the weekly score
options.why: A ranking is relative within the week, so it cannot show whether quality went up or down.

explanation: Pointwise (single-answer) grading gives absolute scores, which suit monitoring a single system over time, provided the rubric, judge prompt and judge model stay fixed. Pairwise comparison is usually more reliable for choosing between two candidates, but it gives relative results only.

stem: An automatic judge consistently prefers longer answers, even when the extra text only restates earlier points. Which two mitigations target this bias? (Choose two.)

options.text: Add rubric criteria that penalise repetition and unsupported padding
options.why: Telling the judge explicitly not to reward padding addresses the bias at its source.

options.text: Statistically control for the length difference when comparing systems
options.why: Length-controlled comparisons predict the preference as if both answers had the same length.

options.text: Use a judge with a longer context window
options.why: Context length decides how much text fits, not whether the judge favours longer answers.

options.text: Truncate every answer to its first 50 words before judging
options.why: Hard truncation cuts real content from good long answers and distorts the comparison.

options.text: Ask the judge to output its verdict before any explanation
options.why: Verdict order does not address the preference for length.

explanation: Verbosity bias is documented for LLM judges: in MT-Bench's repetitive-list test, padded answers fooled weaker judges most of the time. Fixes include explicit rubric criteria (penalise repetition) and length control: Length-Controlled AlpacaEval fits a regression and predicts preferences at zero length difference, raising its correlation with Chatbot Arena from 0.94 to 0.98.

stem: Order the steps to compute the perplexity of a causal language model on a test text.

options.text: Exponentiate the average
Run the model to get the probability of each actual next token given the tokens before it
Tokenize the text with the model's own tokenizer
Average the negative log of those probabilities over all predicted tokens

explanation: Tokenize with the model's tokenizer, score each token's probability given its prefix (for long texts, use a strided sliding window so each token has enough context), average the negative log-likelihoods, and exponentiate. Using disjoint chunks instead of a sliding window gives each token less context and a worse (higher) perplexity.

stem: For a coding problem you generate n = 10 samples and c = 3 pass the tests. Using the unbiased estimator pass@k = 1 - C(n-c, k) / C(n, k), what is pass@2?

options.why: That is 1 - (1 - 0.3)^2, the naive formula, which is biased.

options.text: 0.60, summing two tries
options.why: 0.60 is just 2 x 0.3; probabilities of success over two tries do not add like this.
0.30 is pass@1 (c / n), not pass@2.

explanation: The unbiased estimator draws k of the n samples without replacement: pass@k = 1 - C(n-c, k) / C(n, k). With n = 10, c = 3, k = 2: 1 - 21/45, about 0.533. Generate n >= k samples (the Codex paper used n = 200) and average over problems.

stem: Why did the Codex authors avoid estimating pass@k as 1 - (1 - p)^k, where p is the fraction of samples that passed?

options.text: It is biased: plugging the estimated pass rate into this formula systematically underestimates pass@k
options.why: Correct. The curve is convex in p, so averaging over sampling noise pulls the estimate below the true value.

options.text: It always overestimates pass@k, because it counts the same correct sample several times
options.why: Simulations and the paper's analysis show the plug-in estimate is biased low, not high.

options.text: It cannot be computed when p is exactly 0
options.why: It is defined at p = 0 (it gives 0). Bias, not computability, is the problem.

options.text: It is only valid when k is larger than n
options.why: Both formulas need n >= k; the issue is bias, not this condition.

explanation: With p estimated from n samples, E[1 - (1 - p_hat)^k] is lower than the true 1 - (1 - p)^k, because (1 - x)^k is convex. For example, with true p = 0.2, n = 10 and k = 5, the plug-in averages about 0.59 against a true 0.67, while the unbiased estimator averages 0.67. Use 1 - C(n-c, k) / C(n, k), computed as a running product for numerical stability.

stem: Which two practices reduce LLM-judge bias without collecting new human labels? (Choose two.)

options.text: Evaluate each pair in both orders and treat inconsistent verdicts as ties
options.why: This cancels position bias at the cost of twice as many judge calls.

options.text: Use a judge from a different model family than the systems being compared
options.why: LLM evaluators can recognise and favour their own outputs; a different family reduces self-preference.

options.text: Show the judge which model wrote each answer so it can account for known strengths
options.why: Revealing identities invites brand and self-preference effects; judging should be blind.

options.text: Raise the judge's temperature to average out its biases
options.why: Temperature adds noise around a biased preference; it does not remove the bias.

options.text: Reward longer answers so short, incomplete ones are not preferred
options.why: This amplifies verbosity bias instead of reducing it.

explanation: Common no-label mitigations: swap positions, keep judging blind, use a judge from a different family (self-recognition drives self-preference), length-aware rubrics, and reference-guided grading for maths. You still need some human labels to measure how well the judge agrees with people.

stem: Two annotators label 100 answers as pass or fail. They agree on 80. Each annotator marks 50 answers as pass. What is Cohen's kappa?

options.why: 0.80 is raw agreement; kappa subtracts the agreement expected by chance.
0.50 is the chance agreement here, not kappa.
This does not follow from the formula (0.8 - 0.5) / (1 - 0.5).
Correct. Chance agreement is 0.5 x 0.5 + 0.5 x 0.5 = 0.5, so kappa = (0.8 - 0.5) / 0.5 = 0.6.

explanation: Cohen's kappa = (p_o - p_e) / (1 - p_e), where p_o is observed agreement and p_e is the agreement expected by chance from each rater's label rates. Here p_o = 0.8 and p_e = 0.5, so kappa = 0.6. Kappa is 1 for perfect agreement and 0 for chance-level agreement.

stem: Humans mark 90% of your chatbot's answers as acceptable. A new LLM judge marks every answer as acceptable and agrees with humans 90% of the time. Why is that agreement misleading?

options.text: 90% agreement is too low; judges need 99% before use
options.why: No fixed threshold is the issue; the real problem is that the judge never flags anything.

options.text: It only matches the base rate; Cohen's kappa is 0
options.why: Correct. A constant label matches the majority class, and kappa corrects for that chance agreement.

options.text: Agreement should instead be measured with BLEU between the judge's written explanations and the human reviewers' notes
options.why: BLEU compares wording; agreement on labels needs an agreement statistic such as kappa.

options.text: The judge should be calibrated against another LLM judge instead of humans
options.why: Human labels are the reference you are trying to match; another judge does not fix the problem.

explanation: With a skewed base rate, raw agreement looks high even for a useless judge. Here p_o = 0.9 and p_e = 0.9 x 1.0 + 0.1 x 0 = 0.9, so kappa = 0. Report kappa, and check precision and recall on the minority class (the bad answers you actually want to catch).

stem: A new prompt raised your offline golden-set score from 78% to 84%, but a two-week A/B test shows no change in task completion. What is the most likely explanation to check first?

options.text: The A/B test is broken, because offline scores are always right
options.why: Offline sets are a proxy; when they disagree with real outcomes, the proxy is the first suspect.

options.text: Online metrics are always noisier than offline ones, so you should ship based on the offline result and stop the test
options.why: Noise is a reason to size the test properly, not to ignore it.

options.text: The golden set has drifted from real traffic or been overfitted
options.why: Correct. Check whether the set still matches production queries and whether prompts were tuned against it.

options.text: Task completion cannot be affected by prompts
options.why: Prompts often change task completion; this is not a reason for a null result.

explanation: Offline sets can drift from production traffic, and repeated tuning against the same set overfits it. Refresh the set from recent traffic, keep a held-out portion that is never used for tuning, and check that the online test had enough power to detect the expected effect.

stem: You are launching an LLM feature with no labelled data. Which three steps build a useful first evaluation set quickly? (Choose three.)

options.text: Sample real or realistic user queries, and add hand-written edge cases
options.why: Real inputs give representative coverage, and edge cases cover the failures you most fear.

options.text: Write explicit pass/fail criteria for each kind of case
options.why: Criteria make grading consistent, whether a person or a judge model applies them.

options.text: Check an LLM judge against a small human-labelled subset before trusting it
options.why: Measuring agreement on a subset tells you whether automated grading can be relied on.

options.text: Use a public benchmark such as MMLU as the evaluation set
options.why: Public benchmarks rarely match your users' tasks and may be contaminated.

options.text: Generate 5,000 synthetic questions and accept the model's own answers as ground truth
options.why: Using the model's own answers as truth only measures self-agreement and bakes in its errors.

options.text: Wait until users have labelled 10,000 conversations
options.why: Waiting delays every decision, and users rarely label conversations.

explanation: Without labels, start small and specific: a few hundred real or realistic inputs, deliberately added edge cases and adversarial cases, clear grading criteria, and an LLM judge whose agreement with humans you measure on a subset. Grow the set from production failures over time.

stem: Order the steps for building an evaluation set for a new LLM feature that has no labelled data.

options.text: Collect a sample of real or realistic user inputs
Write explicit grading criteria for each case type
Label a small subset by hand and measure how well an LLM judge agrees with it
Add hand-written edge cases and adversarial inputs
Use the set as a regression gate and add new production failures to it

explanation: Start from real inputs so the set reflects actual use, add edge cases for coverage, define criteria before grading, validate an automated judge against human labels, then use the set to gate changes and keep it fresh with new failures.

stem: Prompts A and B are both run on the same 500 questions. A scores 81.0% and B 83.0%. Each score's 95% confidence interval is about plus or minus 3.4 points, so the intervals overlap. What is the right way to test whether B is better?

options.text: Conclude there is no difference, because the confidence intervals overlap
options.why: Overlapping separate intervals is a conservative test that ignores the pairing, so it can miss real differences.

options.text: Analyse the per-question differences (a paired test), which removes variance from question difficulty
options.why: Correct. Both prompts saw the same questions, so pairing gives a much tighter estimate of the difference.

options.text: Run B on 500 different questions to make the samples independent
options.why: Independent samples add question-to-question variance and make the comparison less precise.

options.text: Repeat the run until B's lead exceeds 5 points, then stop
options.why: Stopping when you like the result inflates false positives.

explanation: When two systems answer the same questions, analyse the per-question score differences (for example a paired t-test or McNemar's test for binary outcomes). Question difficulty affects both systems alike, so pairing removes much of the variance. Report the difference with its standard error and decide the sample size in advance with a power analysis.

stem: A model gets 80% accuracy on 400 independent eval questions. What is the standard error of that accuracy, sqrt(p(1-p)/n)? Give a decimal.
explanation: SE = sqrt(0.8 x 0.2 / 400) = sqrt(0.0004) = 0.02, so a 95% confidence interval is roughly 80% plus or minus 3.9 points. Differences of a point or two between runs on a set this size are within noise. Questions that share a source document are not independent, which makes the real error larger.

stem: A candidate translation is "the the the the" and the single reference is "the cat is on the mat". What is BLEU's modified (clipped) unigram precision?

options.text: 1.0, because every candidate word appears in the reference
options.why: That is unclipped precision. BLEU clips each word's count at its maximum count in a reference.
Correct. "the" appears at most 2 times in the reference, so the clipped count is 2 out of 4 candidate words.
The clip is 2, not 1, because "the" appears twice in the reference.
Precision divides by the candidate's 4 words, not the reference's 6.

explanation: BLEU clips each n-gram count at the most times it appears in any single reference, which stops repeated common words from earning full precision. Here the clipped count is min(4, 2) = 2, so unigram precision is 2/4 = 0.5. BLEU then combines 1- to 4-gram precisions and applies a brevity penalty.

stem: For a fixed set of n samples with c correct, the unbiased pass@k estimate can never go down as k increases (for k up to n).

options.text: True
options.why: Correct. Each extra draw can only add chances to include a passing sample, and the formula reflects that: C(n-c, k) / C(n, k) shrinks as k grows.

options.text: False
options.why: This is wrong: moving from k to k + 1 multiplies the failure term by (n - c - k) / (n - k), which is at most 1, so pass@k never decreases.

explanation: pass@k = 1 - C(n-c, k) / C(n, k). Going from k to k + 1 multiplies the ratio by (n - c - k) / (n - k) <= 1, so the estimate is non-decreasing in k. That is why pass@10 or pass@100 always looks better than pass@1, and why a high pass@k says little unless the product can pick the right sample.

stem: Match each LLM-judge weakness with its most targeted mitigation.

options.text: Judge each pair in both orders
options.why: Removes order effects.

options.text: Control for length or penalise padding in the rubric
options.why: Removes the reward for longer answers.

options.text: Use a judge from a different model family
options.why: Reduces favouritism towards its own outputs.

options.text: Give the judge a reference solution
options.why: Helps the judge check correctness rather than be misled.

prompts.text: Weak grading of maths and reasoning answers

explanation: Each bias needs its own fix: order swaps for position, length control or anti-padding rubrics for verbosity, a different judge family for self-preference, and reference-guided grading for maths, which greatly reduced grading failures in the MT-Bench study.

stem: Two teams report perplexity for the same model on the same test text: 19.4 and 16.4. Both used the model's own tokenizer and the same weights. What most likely explains the gap?

options.text: One team used a GPU and the other a CPU
options.why: Hardware changes tiny floating-point details, not a 3-point perplexity gap.

options.text: Disjoint chunks versus an overlapping sliding window
options.why: Correct. More context per prediction gives lower perplexity; Hugging Face's GPT-2 example shows 19.44 versus 16.44.

options.text: Perplexity is random and varies by about 20% between runs
options.why: Perplexity on a fixed text with fixed weights is deterministic up to tiny numerical noise.

options.text: One team computed the loss in bits and the other in nats, which changes the final perplexity
options.why: Switching log base changes the cross-entropy number, but perplexity is the same whichever base you use consistently.

explanation: For a model with a fixed context length, evaluating disjoint chunks means early tokens in each chunk have little context, which raises perplexity. A strided sliding window gives each token more preceding context; in the Transformers docs, GPT-2 large scored 19.44 with no overlap and 16.44 with stride 512. Always report how perplexity was computed.

stem: A new model beats the old one on public benchmarks and on an LLM-judged leaderboard, but your users, who mostly ask short how-to questions on mobile, say it got worse. Its answers are about twice as long. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: Users dislike change; satisfaction will recover in a few weeks without any action
options.why: Novelty effects exist, but a clear style change is a more specific, testable explanation.

options.text: The benchmarks were too easy, so neither model was really tested
options.why: Easy benchmarks would not explain why users prefer the old model.

options.text: The evaluations reward long answers; these users want short ones
options.why: Correct. The evaluation measures something different from what this audience values.

options.text: The new model's context window is too small for mobile users' questions
options.why: Short how-to questions fit easily in any context window.

explanation: Benchmarks and LLM judges measure particular things (knowledge, verbosity-sensitive preferences) on particular data. When users' tasks and tastes differ, scores and satisfaction diverge. Evaluate on your own traffic, control for length, and confirm with an online test.

stem: A newer model scores higher on public benchmarks, yet your product metrics fall after switching. Which three explanations are plausible? (Choose three.)

options.text: Some benchmark items leaked into its training data, inflating its scores
options.why: Contamination inflates public scores without improving real-world ability.

options.text: Your users' tasks differ from what the benchmarks measure
options.why: Distribution mismatch means benchmark gains need not carry over to your traffic.

options.text: It changed style: longer answers, more refusals or a different format that users dislike
options.why: Style and refusal behaviour affect satisfaction but are barely visible in accuracy benchmarks.

options.text: Benchmarks are averaged over many tasks, which makes their scores exactly match user satisfaction
options.why: Averaging does not make benchmarks match satisfaction; this claims the opposite of the observed gap.

options.text: Higher benchmark scores always cause lower product metrics
options.why: There is no such rule; the relationship is weak, not inverted.

options.text: Your prompts tuned on the old model must be perfect for the new model
options.why: Prompts tuned on one model often need re-tuning for another; assuming they transfer is part of the problem.

explanation: Common causes of the benchmark-versus-users gap: contamination, distribution mismatch, style or verbosity changes, refusal behaviour, latency, and prompts tuned to the old model. The fix is evaluation on your own representative data and an online test before a full switch.

stem: Your assistant's thumbs-up rate is 60%. You want an A/B test that can detect an improvement to 62% with a two-sided 5% significance level and 80% power. Roughly how many rated conversations do you need per arm?

options.text: About 400
options.why: That is enough for a rough accuracy estimate, not to detect a 2-point difference between two rates.

options.text: About 950
options.why: This is off by a factor of ten; small differences between proportions need far more data.

options.text: About 9,300
About 93,000
options.why: This overshoots by a factor of ten for these settings.

explanation: For comparing two proportions, n per arm is about (z_alpha/2 + z_beta)^2 x (p1(1-p1) + p2(1-p2)) / (p2 - p1)^2. With 1.96, 0.84, p1 = 0.60 and p2 = 0.62, that is roughly 9,300. Small effects need large samples; decide n before starting rather than stopping when the result looks good.

stem: You plan to replace human review of chatbot answers with an LLM judge. Which validation plan is most defensible?

options.text: Run the judge on 20 answers and ship if it looks reasonable
options.why: Twenty unstratified answers cannot show agreement per criterion or on rare failure types.

options.text: Measure per-criterion kappa on a stratified human-labelled sample, fix weak criteria, then freeze and re-check
options.why: Correct. This measures agreement where it matters, improves weak criteria, and guards against drift.

options.text: Use the strongest available model as the judge, since frontier-scale judges match human reviewers closely enough to need no validation
options.why: Strong judges still show position, verbosity and self-preference biases; agreement must be measured.

options.text: Ask the judge to rate its own confidence and keep only confident verdicts
options.why: Self-reported confidence is not validated agreement with humans.

explanation: Treat an LLM judge as a classifier that needs validation: human labels on a stratified sample, agreement statistics per criterion (kappa, plus precision and recall on failures), rubric iteration, and a frozen judge configuration so scores stay comparable. Re-validate when the judge model or rubric changes.

stem: Your CI runs a 300-case LLM regression suite on every prompt change. Scores move by 1 to 2 points between identical runs, so the gate keeps failing at random. Which two changes make the gate trustworthy? (Choose two.)

options.text: Pin the judge model and prompt, and run several samples per case
options.why: A fixed judge removes one source of drift, and repeated samples average out sampling noise.

options.text: Fail only on statistically significant drops against the baseline, plus any failure on a small set of critical cases
options.why: A significance threshold separates real regressions from noise, while must-pass cases protect what matters most.

options.text: Lower the pass threshold until the gate never fails
options.why: A gate that never fails catches no regressions.

options.text: Remove the gate and rely on manual review
options.why: This throws away automated protection instead of fixing the noise.

options.text: Set temperature to 0 everywhere, which makes outputs bit-identical
options.why: Temperature 0 reduces but does not guarantee identical outputs on shared servers, and it hides variance users see.

explanation: LLM evaluations are noisy: sampling, judge variance and server non-determinism all move scores. A robust gate pins the judge configuration, uses repeated samples or paired comparisons against the baseline, applies a significance threshold, and keeps a small set of must-pass critical cases.

stem: Which two practices keep an internal golden evaluation set trustworthy over time? (Choose two.)

options.text: Keep a held-out portion that is never used while tuning prompts
options.why: A split nobody tunes against stays an honest estimate of generalisation.

options.text: Regularly add new cases drawn from recent production failures and traffic
options.why: This keeps the set aligned with real usage as it drifts.

options.text: Keep editing prompts until every case passes, then treat 100% as proof of quality
options.why: Tuning until the set is perfect overfits it; a perfect score then says little about new inputs.

options.text: Publish the full set on a public website for transparency
options.why: Public sets can leak into training data of future models, contaminating them.

options.text: Delete cases that always fail, because they lower the average
options.why: Persistent failures are the most informative cases; removing them hides real weaknesses.

explanation: Golden sets decay in two ways: overfitting (prompts tuned against them) and drift (production traffic changes). Keep a held-out split, refresh from production, version the set, and keep hard cases even when they hurt the average.

stem: A code assistant shows users exactly one suggestion per request, with no test run before display. Offline you measure pass@1 = 45% and pass@10 = 80%. Which number best predicts the user experience, and when would the other matter?

options.text: pass@10, because it shows the model's full potential
options.why: Users see one suggestion, so the potential of ten samples is not delivered to them.

options.text: pass@1; pass@10 matters only if you generate several candidates and have a way, such as tests, to pick a correct one
options.why: Correct. pass@k assumes some way of choosing among the k samples.

options.text: Their average, 62.5%, because users sometimes accept the first suggestion and sometimes regenerate
options.why: Averaging two different quantities gives a number that describes no real scenario.

options.text: Neither; only BLEU against reference code predicts user experience
options.why: BLEU is a poor proxy for functional correctness, as the HumanEval authors showed.

explanation: pass@k is the chance that at least one of k samples is correct. It reflects the product only if the product can find that sample, for example by running tests or letting the user pick. With one unverified suggestion per request, pass@1 is the relevant number.

stem: You validate an LLM judge on 100 answers. Humans pass 80 and the judge passes 70. They agree on 76 answers (63 both pass, 13 both fail). What is Cohen's kappa? Round to two decimal places.
explanation: Observed agreement p_o = 0.76. Chance agreement p_e = 0.8 x 0.7 + 0.2 x 0.3 = 0.62. Kappa = (0.76 - 0.62) / (1 - 0.62) = 0.14 / 0.38, about 0.37. A 76% raw agreement sounds good, but most of it is expected by chance when both raters pass most answers, so this judge needs a better rubric before it replaces human review.

stem: Order the stages for safely rolling out a new model behind an existing LLM feature.

options.text: Run a randomised A/B test with guardrail metrics such as latency, cost and complaint rate
Score the candidate offline on the golden set and critical regression cases
Roll out fully and keep monitoring online quality metrics
Shadow or canary it on a small slice of real traffic and review its outputs

explanation: Offline evaluation is cheap and catches obvious regressions; shadow or canary traffic reveals production issues at low risk; an A/B test measures real impact with guardrails; full rollout continues with monitoring so drift is caught later.

stem: Your LLM judge scores support answers on a 1 to 10 "overall quality" scale. Scores cluster at 7 to 8, barely separate good from bad answers, and two runs often disagree. What rubric change helps most?

options.text: Switch to a 1 to 100 scale for finer resolution
options.why: A wider scale adds false precision; vague criteria remain the problem.

options.text: Replace it with several defined yes/no checks, each with examples
options.why: Correct. Narrow, well-defined binary checks are easier to judge consistently and show what failed.

options.text: Ask the judge to be stricter
options.why: A vague instruction shifts the scores but does not make them more consistent.

options.text: Average the scores of three different judge models that all use the same holistic 1 to 10 rubric
options.why: Averaging reduces noise somewhat but keeps the vague, low-information criteria.

explanation: Holistic numeric scales give clustered, noisy scores. Break quality into specific criteria with clear pass/fail definitions and examples; each criterion becomes easier to judge reliably, easier to validate against humans, and easier to act on.

stem: Your evaluation set has 50 source documents with 10 questions about each (500 questions total). A teammate computes the standard error as if all 500 questions were independent. What is the problem?

options.text: Nothing; 500 questions is large enough for any method
options.why: Sample size does not fix a wrong independence assumption.

options.text: Questions about the same document are correlated, so the naive standard error is too small; use clustered standard errors by document
options.why: Correct. Effective sample size is closer to the number of documents than the number of questions.

options.text: The standard error should be computed separately for each question and then summed across all 500 questions
options.why: Summing per-question errors is not a valid way to combine them.

options.text: Standard errors only apply to multiple-choice questions
options.why: They apply to any averaged score, including judge-graded open answers.

explanation: When questions share a passage or topic, their results are correlated, and treating them as independent understates uncertainty. Clustered standard errors (clustered by document) give honest error bars; Miller's 'Adding Error Bars to Evals' recommends this along with paired comparisons and power analysis.

stem: A summarisation model learns to append extra sentences restating the source, and its ROUGE recall against reference summaries goes up. What does this show about using ROUGE recall as the target?

options.text: Nothing; higher ROUGE recall always means better summaries
options.why: Recall rewards covering reference words, which padding can do without improving the summary.

options.text: Recall alone rewards padding; add precision, length limits and rubric checks
options.why: Correct. For example, a 10-word output containing all 6 reference words has recall 1.0 but precision only 0.6.

options.text: ROUGE should be replaced by perplexity for summaries
options.why: Perplexity measures predictability, not whether a summary is faithful or concise.

options.text: ROUGE recall already penalises longer outputs through its brevity term, so the model must have improved
options.why: Recall divides by the reference length, so extra output words are never penalised.

explanation: ROUGE was designed as a recall-oriented metric: overlap divided by the reference's n-gram count. Longer outputs can only add overlap, so optimising recall alone rewards padding. Use F-measure, length constraints and faithfulness or rubric checks, and remember that n-gram overlap misses paraphrase and factual errors.
